summary: Similar shapes are scaled copies: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides shares one ratio (the scale factor). Learners find the scale factor from a known matched pair (new ÷ old), then multiply the other sides by that same factor (a factor greater than 1 enlarges; a factor less than 1, such as 1/3, reduces — equivalently, when reducing you can divide by the enlargement factor). The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive — adding a constant to each side generally distorts the shape (e.g. any non-square rectangle; a square or equilateral triangle is an exception) — and that a length scale factor k scales area by k² (and volume by k³ for solids).
misconceptions: Additive enlargement — adding the same amount to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor (distorts the shape; the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error).
Treating 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or as 'congruent/identical', not checking that all sides share one ratio.
Believing that doubling the lengths doubles the area (area actually scales by k²; MAP Enlargements documents this as a persistent error).
Applying the scale factor to only one side, or using new÷old for one pair and old÷new for another (inconsistent direction).

activities.title: Enlargement studio: grab, scale, and compare with additive mode
steps: Work on a grid with a non-square rectangle or triangle whose aspect ratio is locked. Drag a corner to enlarge it and watch a live scale-factor readout while every side multiplies by the same factor and the angles stay unchanged; for a rectangle enlarged from a fixed corner, notice the dragged opposite corner moves along the original's diagonal, showing it is the same shape.
Fill a ratio table alongside (old side | new side for each pair) and check that the same column multiplier appears for every pair of corresponding sides.

Flip to an 'additive mode' that instead ADDS your chosen number to each side of the non-square rectangle; observe it stretch lopsided and fall off the original's diagonal — it is no longer similar. Compare directly with the multiplicative result.
Turn on a grid-tiling overlay: with a scale factor of 2, see FOUR copies of the original tile the new shape; with a factor of 3, nine copies fit — connect this to area × k².
If a scaling touches only one side, use the flag that highlights the unchanged side and correct it so every corresponding side is scaled.
activities.insight: Enlargement multiplies every corresponding side by the SAME factor, preserving shape and angles; adding the same amount to each side of a non-square rectangle distorts it. Because the shape grows in two dimensions, area scales by k², not by k.

activities.title: Confront the additive error on paper
steps: Take a 2×5 rectangle. Add 4 to each side to get a 6×9 rectangle, and draw both. Check whether the side ratios match: 2:5 versus 6:9 — they do not, so the shapes are not similar.
Now enlarge the same 2×5 rectangle by a scale factor, multiplying each side by 3 to get 6×15, and confirm 2:5 and 6:15 are the same ratio.
State in your own words why 'add the same to each side' changes the shape while 'multiply each side by the same number' keeps it.
activities.insight: Adding a constant to every side changed the proportions of the 2×5 rectangle (as it does for any non-square rectangle); multiplying every side by a common factor always keeps corresponding sides in a single ratio and preserves the shape.

activities.title: Solve and judge similar-shape problems
steps: Given a rectangle 6×9 enlarged so 6→18, find the scale factor (18 ÷ 6 = 3) and the missing side (9 × 3 = 27 cm). Beware of adding the difference 12 to get 21 — that is the additive error, not a valid answer.
Find the scale factor between two similar triangles from a matched pair of side lengths, keeping new ÷ old consistent for the comparison.

Judge whether two given shapes are similar by testing EVERY pair of corresponding sides for the same ratio, not by appearance, and by checking that corresponding angles are equal (for triangles, matching side ratios are enough; for other polygons they are not, e.g. a square and a non-square rhombus). One mismatched ratio means not similar.

For a REDUCTION (e.g. 18 back to 6), decide first whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the side you start from; then divide by the enlargement factor (÷3), which is the same as multiplying by the new ÷ old factor (6 ÷ 18 = 1/3).
On an area follow-up for the 6×9→18×27 rectangle, reason that area scales by k² = 3² = 9 (54 cm² → 486 cm²), not by 3.
activities.insight: Problem solving means finding the scale factor from a known pair, applying it in the correct direction to every side, checking similarity by shared ratio, and using k² for area.

activities.title: Optional extension: scaling a solid to feel k² and k³
steps: Enlarge a cube or cuboid with a slider and watch surface area grow by k² and volume by k³.
Fill the enlarged solid with unit cubes to count that doubling every edge of a cube gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and relate the growing faces to k² area.
Return to a flat similar-shapes problem and restate: length ×k, area ×k², and for solids volume ×k³.
activities.insight: Scaling length by k scales area by k² and, for solids, volume by k³ — the same multiplicative idea extended by dimension.

checkQuestion: Here is a rectangle 6 cm by 9 cm. I enlarge it so the 6 cm side becomes 18 cm, and the new rectangle is similar to the old one. Work out the length of the other side. Show your working.
checkAnswer: 27 cm. The scale factor is 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so every side is multiplied by 3: the 9 cm side becomes 9 × 3 = 27 cm.
